stem: A client with type 1 diabetes says, “I’m exhausted by the constant decisions about glucose, insulin, food, and activity, and I feel overwhelmed by diabetes every day.” The client does not describe persistent loss of interest or other symptoms sufficient to establish a depressive disorder. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: The client may be experiencing diabetes distress, an emotional burden specifically related to living with and managing diabetes that is distinct from depression or anxiety.
options.B: The statement establishes major depressive disorder because diabetes distress and depression are the same diagnosis.
options.C: Diabetes distress occurs only near the time of diagnosis and is unlikely after years of diabetes self-management.
options.D: The concern is not clinically relevant unless the client first develops a diabetes complication.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care define diabetes distress as emotional burdens and worries associated with living with and managing a demanding chronic condition. Diabetes distress is distinct from depression and anxiety, although they can coexist. The ongoing demands of medication dosing, glucose monitoring, food decisions, and physical activity can contribute to distress. ADA recommends screening for diabetes distress at least annually and repeating screening when treatment goals are not met, at transitional times, or when complications occur. B incorrectly equates distinct conditions. C is false because distress can occur throughout the diabetes course. D incorrectly minimizes a concern that should be acknowledged and addressed even without a complication.
educational_objective: Recognize diabetes distress as a diabetes-specific emotional burden distinct from depressive or anxiety disorders and identify it as a clinically relevant concern that warrants routine assessment and support.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Psychosocial Care — Diabetes Distress, Recommendation 5.45 and accompanying text: screen at least annually and at other critical times; diabetes distress refers to emotional burdens and worries associated with living with/managing diabetes, is distinct from depression and anxiety, and is associated with the constant behavioral demands of diabetes self-management
source_claim_supported: Diabetes distress is a diabetes-specific emotional burden related to the ongoing demands of self-management, is distinct from depression/anxiety, can occur throughout the disease course, and should be routinely assessed and addressed.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — assess emotional responses to illness, provide therapeutic support, and recognize psychosocial factors affecting health and self-management
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — diabetes distress and chronic-disease self-management burden
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source definition-only item into a clinical recognition scenario. The final version uses the exact ADA 2026 distinction between diabetes distress and depression/anxiety, avoids treating distress as a psychiatric diagnosis, and preserves its relevance across the diabetes course rather than only at diagnosis.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 5, Recommendation 5.45 and the diabetes-distress subsection. The definition, distinction from depression/anxiety, routine screening recommendation, and self-management burden are explicit.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses ADA-supported diabetes-specific emotional-burden language and avoids diagnosing a psychiatric disorder. The stem deliberately lacks sufficient depressive-disorder criteria so B cannot be a second answer.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; the described burden is consistent with diabetes distress.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; diabetes distress and major depressive disorder are distinct constructs and require different assessment.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; distress is not limited to the period around diagnosis.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; distress warrants assessment and support independent of whether a complication is already present.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A fits the diabetes-specific emotional burden while respecting the absence of evidence needed to diagnose depression.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are psychosocial interpretations of the same client statement and use similar clinical scope.
audit_findings.blueprint: Psychosocial Integrity is directly aligned because the nurse is recognizing an emotional response to chronic illness and self-management burden.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked diabetes-distress definition, depression/anxiety distinction, screening timing, diagnosis-versus-screening scope, chronic-course applicability, distractor plausibility, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
